maps.title: The world of the first Christians
maps.intro: The places that matter most in this era, from Jerusalem to Rome. Region names are the Roman ones used in Acts and Paul's letters.

maps.title: First journey
maps.intro: Acts says the church at Antioch sent out Barnabas and Paul. They crossed Cyprus, then went inland to cities in the Roman province of Galatia, in the regions Acts calls Pisidia and Lycaonia, and came back the same way.

maps.title: Ignatius on the road to Rome
maps.intro: Eusebius says Ignatius was sent from Syria to Rome under military guard, and that he wrote from Smyrna and from Troas. Polycarp's letter speaks of the patience the Philippians had seen in Ignatius, which suggests he passed through Philippi. The sources used here do not record the rest of the way, so the lines between these stops are straight and show only the order.

maps.title: The First Crusade, 1096 to 1099
maps.intro: The route of the crusading armies from Constantinople to Jerusalem, drawn straight between places, with the sieges and battles that marked it. Gibbon traces the march across Asia Minor by Dorylaeum, Iconium and Erekli (Heraclea); Tancred and Baldwin turned aside to Tarsus, and Baldwin went on to Edessa.

stops.ref: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), 'Crusades'; Gibbon, chapter 58; Schaff, vol. 5, § 50
stops.note: Besieged for seven weeks, Gibbon says. The emperor Alexius had it surrendered to himself and kept the crusaders out, in June 1097 (1 June in the Catholic Encyclopedia, 19 June in Schaff)
The Turks surprise one of the two crusading columns; the crusaders defeat them on 1 July 1097
Reached on 20 October 1097 and taken on the night of 2 June 1098; the next day the crusaders are besieged inside it, until they drive off Kerbogha's army on 28 June
Besieged from 7 June 1099 and entered on 15 July; the crusaders kill its inhabitants, the Catholic Encyclopedia says
An Egyptian army is defeated here on 12 August 1099

maps.title: The Third Crusade, 1189 to 1192
maps.intro: Richard I's route by sea from Messina, by way of Cyprus, to Acre and Jaffa, drawn straight between places. Frederick Barbarossa's army went overland and took Iconium, and he drowned crossing the river Selef (Kalykadnos) in the Taurus region in 1190. Hattin, where Saladin defeated the army of Jerusalem in 1187, is marked for background.

stops.name: Cyprus
stops.note: Shipwrecked on the coast in 1191, Richard conquers the island from Isaac Comnenus

stops.name: Acre
stops.note: Besieged from June 1189; it capitulates on 13 July 1191, after the kings of France and England arrive, and becomes the crusaders' base
Richard defends it against Saladin in 1192; after a truce he sails for Europe on 9 October 1192, without having entered Jerusalem

maps.intro: Conrad III and Louis VII cross Anatolia, meet at Nicaea and go on to Ephesus; Louis sails from Attalia to Antioch, and the crusade fails before Damascus in July 1148. Edessa, whose fall in 1144 led to the crusade, is marked. The route is drawn straight between places and is simplified.

stops.note: The German and French kings meet here in 1147 and go on together to Ephesus
